items.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...something would come up like “A Walk in the Black Forest,” by Horst Jankowski I think his name was...

ctx.x: Oh yeah, there were a lot of them. As a matter of fact I wasted about two years of my life trying to find a way to stop them from doing it. And I had attorneys and copyright attorneys and regular attorneys, and we did a lot of research. We found out, they found out that I couldn’t — it’s different now, you can copyright arrangements now — well you could in those days but it was a very complicated thing I ran into. I finally found that the best thing for me to do was to forget about all the imitators, and just…

It seems that the instrumental sound at that time — let me rephrase that — we don’t hear as many instrumental hits anymore you know. You had your music and every once in a while something would come up like “A Walk in the Black Forest,” by Horst Jankowski I think his name was, and then of course the Tijuana Brass. And that it was still possible to have instrumental music be big sellers. I don’t know where that fell by the wayside. I don’t think we hear that that much anymore, just purely instrumental music,…
Yeah. The last one I can really thing of [scats].
